questions.q: Propene is refluxed with N-bromosuccinimide in anhydrous CCl₄ under light. The organic product is:
questions.explain: NBS with light replaces an allylic hydrogen by Br and leaves the C=C intact, giving allyl bromide with succinimide as the by-product. It is a radical substitution, not an addition.

questions.q: Cyclohexene is treated separately with (P) Br₂ in CCl₄ in the dark at room temperature and (Q) NBS, hν, CCl₄. The products of P and Q are respectively:
questions.explain: Br₂ in the dark adds across C=C to give the vicinal dibromide, while NBS with light substitutes at the allylic CH₂ to give 3-bromocyclohexene. Reading the reagent decides between addition and substitution.

questions.q: Why is NBS preferred to Br₂ for allylic bromination of an alkene?
options: NBS is a stronger brominating agent than Br₂
NBS adds to C=C faster than Br₂
NBS keeps the Br₂ and HBr concentration very low, so radical substitution wins over ionic addition
NBS converts the alkene into a carbocation first
questions.explain: NBS acts as a bromine reservoir: HBr formed in the chain regenerates small amounts of Br₂ from NBS. Addition across C=C needs a high Br₂ concentration, so at low concentration allylic substitution takes over.

questions.q: In the accepted (Goldfinger) mechanism of the Wohl–Ziegler reaction, the species that removes the allylic hydrogen is:
questions.explain: Br• abstracts the allylic H to give the resonance-stabilised allyl radical and HBr. The older picture with a succinimidyl N• radical is rejected because the N–Br bond is much stronger than Br–Br.
